package_info.package_name: UNSTABLE, Condi, Skibidi (Mirai variants and DDoS botnets)
package_info.package_manager: Linux binary malware (distributed via cloud, not traditional package manager)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple binaries for various architectures (e.g., x86_64, mips, armv7l, etc.)
package_info.why_malicious: These malware families are designed to exploit known vulnerabilities in network devices, establish command and control (C2) connections via cloud infrastructure, perform brute-force attacks, conduct DDoS attacks, and exfiltrate process and system information. They leverage cloud services for distribution and C2, making detection and takedown more difficult. The malware is distributed as unsanctioned binaries for multiple architectures, enabling rapid propagation across diverse IoT and Linux-based devices.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Downloader script fetches multiple binaries for 13 architectures and executes them with the parameter 'jaws.exploit'.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At exploit-time (post-exploitation), the script downloads multiple architecture-specific binaries from an external IP and executes them with exploit-specific parameters, enabling remote code execution and further infection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated download and execution of binaries from an external, non-trusted source is a hallmark of malware propagation, especially when targeting multiple architectures.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not download and execute arbitrary binaries post-exploitation, particularly from hardcoded, untrusted IP addresses.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated update scripts in legitimate software, but these are signed and sourced from trusted, verified servers.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Hardcoded brute-force list of usernames and passwords used for scanning and attacking other endpoints.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (scanner module execution), the malware iterates through a hardcoded list of credentials to attempt brute-force logins on other network devices, enabling lateral movement and further infections.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Use of a large, hardcoded credential list for automated network scanning and brute-force attacks is a classic sign of botnet propagation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not perform brute-force credential attacks across the network.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testing tools (with explicit authorization and in controlled environments).

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: attack_tcp_ack, attack_tcp_syn, attack_tcp_legit, attack_tcp_sack2, attack_udp_plain, attack_udp_vse, attack_udp_thread, attack_gre_ip, attack_method_nudp
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (upon receiving C2 command), the malware launches various DDoS attacks using multiple protocols, generating high volumes of malicious traffic to overwhelm target systems.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Presence of multiple DDoS attack methods, each targeting different network protocols, is a clear indicator of botnet malware designed for denial-of-service operations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not include routines for launching DDoS attacks or responding to C2 commands to initiate such attacks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Network stress testing tools (used with explicit consent and in controlled environments).
key_indicators: Multiple DDoS routines (TCP, UDP, GRE, etc.)
Ability to flood targets with protocol-specific traffic

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Kills off competing malware and specific processes, then connects to C2 server 'trembolone[.]zapto[.]org'.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (upon infection), the malware terminates other malware and specific processes, then establishes a persistent connection to a C2 server using a dynamic DNS domain, ensuring exclusive control and ongoing communication.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware often kills competing processes to maintain exclusive control over the infected device and ensure persistence, while connecting to dynamic DNS C2 domains for flexible command and control.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not terminate unrelated processes or connect to suspicious C2 domains, especially via dynamic DNS.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System management tools may terminate processes, but only with user authorization and never in conjunction with C2 communication.
key_indicators: Process termination logic targeting other malware
C2 connection to dynamic DNS domain

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Usage: %s <IP> <SECONDS> [PORT] ... triggers UDP flooding DoS attack using random characters.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (when executed with target parameters), the tool sends a continuous stream of UDP packets with randomized payloads to the specified IP and port for a set duration, causing denial of service.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Purpose-built DoS tools that generate high-volume UDP floods are inherently malicious when distributed outside of controlled, authorized environments.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal binaries do not perform network flooding attacks or accept parameters to target arbitrary IPs for DoS.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Network stress testing (with explicit authorization and in isolated test environments).
key_indicators: UDP flood logic with randomized payloads
Command-line interface for targeting arbitrary IPs

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Creates socket, checks C2 server reachability, executes 'ps -eo pid,comm --no-headers' via /bin/bash, reads /proc/<PID>/comm, sends info to C2.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (post-infection), the malware enumerates running processes by executing system commands and reading process information, then exfiltrates the collected data to the C2 server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Process enumeration and exfiltration of system information to an external server is a common reconnaissance and persistence technique in malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not exfiltrate process lists or system information to external, untrusted servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System monitoring tools may collect process information, but do not transmit it externally without user consent.
key_indicators: Network exfiltration of process and system info

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Displays 'youre not skibidi enough', calls ptrace to fork and evade detection, decodes XOR-encoded strings, calls prctl to rename process, connects to C2, uses select to monitor events, sends results to C2.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (upon execution), the malware displays a decoy message, employs anti-analysis techniques (ptrace), decodes obfuscated strings, renames its process using prctl, establishes a C2 connection, monitors process events, and exfiltrates results to the C2 server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Anti-analysis (ptrace), process renaming (prctl), persistent C2 communication, and event monitoring are advanced malware behaviors designed for stealth and long-term control.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not evade debugging, rename itself to mimic system processes, or maintain persistent C2 connections for exfiltration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Security tools may use anti-debugging or process renaming, but not in conjunction with C2 communication and event exfiltration.
key_indicators: prctl process renaming to mimic system processes

attack_chain.action: Exploit device vulnerabilities (e.g., CVE-2016-20016, CVE-2023-1389, CVE-2024-21887) to gain initial access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Downloader script execution and malware deployment

attack_chain.action: Downloader script fetches and executes architecture-specific malware binaries.
Malware performs brute-force scanning of network devices using hardcoded credentials.
Malware establishes C2 connection, kills competing processes, and prepares for attack.
On C2 command, malware launches DDoS attacks using various protocols.
Malware enumerates running processes and exfiltrates information to C2.
Advanced evasion and persistence techniques (anti-debugging, process renaming, event monitoring, C2 communication).

behavioral_signatures: Automated download and execution of binaries from external IPs post-exploitation
Brute-force scanning with hardcoded credential lists targeting network devices
Process enumeration and exfiltration of system/process information to external servers
Multiple DDoS attack routines (TCP, UDP, GRE, etc.) triggered by C2 commands
Process killing of competing malware and unrelated processes
Anti-debugging (ptrace) and process renaming (prctl) to evade detection
Persistent C2 communication using cloud infrastructure and dynamic DNS domains
Decoding of XOR-obfuscated strings for runtime configuration
file_indicators: Presence of binaries for multiple architectures in /tmp or other writable directories
Process names set to '-bash', 'x86_64' via prctl
Malware binaries retrieved from /getters/ paths on suspicious IPs
network_indicators: Outbound connections to /getters/ paths on suspicious IPs
Unusual high-volume UDP or TCP traffic to external IPs (indicative of DDoS)
Persistent outbound connections to dynamic DNS domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unauthorized downloads and execution of binaries from external IPs, especially following exploitation of known device vulnerabilities. Detect brute-force login attempts using common credentials across network devices. Watch for process enumeration and exfiltration behaviors, as well as persistent connections to known C2 IPs and dynamic DNS domains. Look for process renaming and anti-debugging techniques in running processes. Correlate network traffic to known malicious infrastructure, including /getters/ paths and high-volume UDP/TCP traffic, and block or alert on these indicators. Implement file integrity monitoring for the appearance of suspicious binaries in writable directories.
